title: Vowel Harmony
subtitle: Balancing front and back vowels across Finnish suffixes
keyPoint: Finnish words with back vowels (a, o, u) take back-vowel endings, while words with front vowels (ä, ö, y) take front-vowel endings, with e and i being neutral.

mistakes.note: Helsinki contains front/neutral vowels only, so it requires -ssä instead of -ssa.
Pöytä contains the front vowel ö, so the suffix must be -llä.
Tyttö has y and ö, so all attached endings must obey front vowel harmony.

quiz.question: Choose the correct ending for 'in the sauna' (sauna + inessive):
quiz.explanation: 'Sauna' contains back vowels (a, u), so it takes the back suffix -ssa.

quiz.question: Choose the correct form for 'on the table' (pöytä + adessive):
quiz.explanation: 'Pöytä' has front vowels (ö, y) and weakens t to d, requiring -llä.

quiz.question: Choose the correct form for 'in the city' (kaupunki + inessive):
quiz.explanation: 'Kaupunki' contains back vowels (a, u), requiring -ssa after consonant gradation.

quiz.question: Choose the correct form for 'in the woods' (metsä + inessive):
quiz.explanation: 'Metsä' contains ä, a front vowel, so it takes -ssä.

tip: Neutral vowels e and i can appear with any vowel, but if a word has ONLY e and i (like 'tie' or 'kieli'), treat it as a front-vowel word (-ssä/-llä).

title: Consonant Gradation (K-P-T Alternation)
subtitle: Alternating between strong and weak stems in Finnish
keyPoint: The consonants k, p, and t change between strong and weak grades when suffixes close or open a syllable.

mistakes.note: Single 't' weakens to 'd' in the adessive case (-lla).
Double 'kk' weakens to single 'k' in the genitive case (-n).
The verb lukea weakens k to nothing in the first person singular: minä luen.

quiz.question: Complete with the correct form: 'Hän asuu tällä ___.' (katu)
quiz.explanation: In katu, the single t weakens to d when -lla is added.

quiz.question: Complete with the correct form: 'Minä ___ lehteä.' (lukea)
quiz.explanation: The verb lukea drops 'k' in the first-person singular: minä luen.

quiz.question: Complete with the correct form: 'Kenen tämä ___ on?' (hattu + genitive -n)
quiz.explanation: The double tt weakens to a single t: hatun.

quiz.question: Complete with the correct form: 'Juon kahvia punaisesta ___.' (kuppi + -sta)
quiz.explanation: Double pp weakens to single p in the weak grade: kupista.

tip: Double consonants (kk, pp, tt) always weaken to singles (k, p, t), which makes them the easiest gradation patterns to spot!

title: The Six Verb Types and Present Conjugation
subtitle: Stem patterns and personal endings for Finnish verbs
keyPoint: Finnish verbs fall into six distinct infinitive types, each revealing how to extract the present stem before adding personal endings.

mistakes.note: Type 3 verbs drop the infinitive marker (-la) and insert an connecting 'e': tul + e + n.
The verb puhua requires the partitive case for languages.
Type 4 verbs change -t- to vocalic stem halua- before adding personal endings (-mme).

quiz.question: Select the correct form: 'Minä ___ teetä.' (juoda, Type 2)
quiz.explanation: Type 2 verbs drop -da/-dä: juo- + -n = juon.

quiz.question: Select the correct form: 'Me ___ Helsingissä.' (asua, Type 1)
quiz.explanation: The personal ending for 'me' (we) is -mme: asumme.

quiz.question: Select the correct form: 'Mitä sinä ___?' (tehdä, irregular/Type 2)
quiz.explanation: Tehdä has the present stem tee-; with 'sinä' ending -t, it becomes teet.

quiz.question: Select the correct form: 'He ___ bussipysäkillä.' (seisoa, Type 1)
quiz.explanation: The 3rd person plural (he) ending is -vat/-vät: seisovat.

tip: The standard personal endings (-n, -t, -vowel/-see, -mme, -tte, -vat/-vät) stay consistent across almost all verb types once you find the stem!

title: Internal vs. External Locative Cases
subtitle: Navigating -s- and -l- spatial case endings in Finnish
keyPoint: Internal locatives (-ssa, -sta, -on/-in) indicate containment inside an enclosed space, while external locatives (-lla, -lta, -lle) indicate position on an open surface or proximity.

mistakes.note: A book rests on top of a table surface (-lla), not trapped inside the table structure (-ssa).

mistakes.wrong: Olen töissä asemalla ja asun Tampereella.
mistakes.right: Olen töissä asemalla ja asun Tampereella.
mistakes.note: City names vary: Helsinki uses Helsingissä (-ssä), but Tampere traditionally uses Tampereella (-lla).
Movement towards an open station venue takes the allative case (-lle).

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Maito on ___.' (jääkaappi - inside)
quiz.explanation: Milk is inside the refrigerator, requiring the inessive case (-ssa/-ssä with consonant gradation: pp -> p).

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Laitatko lautasen ___?' (pöytä - onto)
quiz.explanation: Putting something onto a surface uses the allative case (-lle): pöydälle.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Me tulemme kotiin ___.' (koulu - out from school)
quiz.explanation: Leaving an enclosed building uses the elative case (-sta): koulusta.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Bussi saapuu kohta ___.' (pysäkki - to the stop)
quiz.explanation: An open station or bus stop takes the external allative case (-lle): pysäkille.

tip: Think of S-cases as a closed box (in, out of, into) and L-cases as a flat tabletop or open field (on, off of, onto)!

title: The Partitive Case (Partitiivi) in Basic Contexts
subtitle: Expressing indefinite amounts, negatives, and quantities
keyPoint: The partitive case (-a/-ä, -ta/-tä, -tta/-ttä) is used for indefinite quantities, after numbers greater than one, and for objects in negative sentences.

cells: En osta leipää (I don't buy bread)
Luen lehteä (I am reading a paper)

mistakes.note: Numbers higher than one require the noun in the singular partitive case (-a/-ä).
Direct objects of negative sentences must always take the partitive case.
Uncountable substances like water require the partitive case (vesi -> vettä).

quiz.question: Complete the negative sentence: 'Minä en tunne tuota ___.' (mies)
quiz.explanation: In negative sentences, the direct object takes the partitive case: miestä.

quiz.question: Complete with the correct number construction: 'Pihalla seisoo neljä ___.' (poika)
quiz.explanation: Numbers greater than one require the following noun in the singular partitive: poikaa.

quiz.question: Complete with the correct partitive form: 'Haluatko lisää ___?' (kahvi)
quiz.explanation: Uncountable drinks and foods take the partitive ending -a/-ä: kahvia.

quiz.question: Complete the negative sentence: 'Meillä ei ole ___.' (talo)
quiz.explanation: Negative existential sentences require the subject to appear in the partitive: taloa.

tip: Always remember the golden rule: if a sentence has 'ei' (negative verb), its object almost always transforms into the partitive case!

title: Possession Structure ('Minulla on')
subtitle: Expressing ownership with the adessive case and 'olla'
keyPoint: Finnish has no verb 'to have'; instead, it uses the owner in the adessive case (-lla/-llä) followed by the 3rd person singular verb 'on' or 'ei ole'.

useCases.label: Negative Possession
useCases.example: Meillä ei ole paljon aikaa tänään.

mistakes.note: Finnish does not have an active transitive verb for 'to have'; you must use the adessive ending -lla/-llä + on.
The verb olla remains strictly in the 3rd person singular 'on', even when the possessed items are plural.
In negative possession clauses, the item that is not possessed must be placed in the partitive case.

quiz.question: I have a cat.
quiz.explanation: The owner takes the adessive case suffix -lla ('Minulla') and the verb is always 3rd person singular 'on'.

quiz.question: Do you (singular) have a car?
quiz.explanation: In an affirmative question asking about a whole count noun, the noun is nominative and the question verb 'onko' comes first.

quiz.question: He does not have time.
quiz.explanation: Negative possession uses the adessive owner + 'ei ole' + the possessed noun in the partitive case ('aikaa').

quiz.question: We have three dogs.
quiz.explanation: Even with multiple items, the verb stays singular 'on', and numbers above one require a partitive singular noun ('kolme koiraa').

tip: Always remember: the verb in this structure is fixed as 'on' (or 'ei ole') in the present tense, never change it to 'ovat'!

title: Total vs. Partial Objects (Accusative vs. Partitive)
subtitle: Choosing between complete and ongoing actions or quantities
keyPoint: Use the partitive case for ongoing processes, indefinite amounts, and negative sentences; use the accusative (-n or nominative shape) for completed actions affecting a whole object.

cells: I am reading the book (in progress)

mistakes.note: Any direct object in a negative sentence MUST be in the partitive case without exception.
If an action is currently incomplete or ongoing ('right now'), use the partitive case, not the genitive-accusative.
In 1st and 2nd person imperatives, total objects drop the -n suffix and take the nominative form.

quiz.question: I am drinking milk right now (ongoing process).
quiz.explanation: An ongoing process or continuous consumption of an indefinite mass noun requires the partitive case ('maitoa').

quiz.question: I drank (all of) the milk.
quiz.explanation: The past completed action affecting a specified full quantity takes the genitive-accusative ending -n ('maidon').

quiz.question: I did not buy the computer.
quiz.explanation: The object of any negated verb is always in the partitive case ('tietokonetta').

quiz.question: Read this text! (Imperative singular)
quiz.explanation: Total objects with imperative forms do not take the -n suffix; they take the nominative form ('tämä teksti').

tip: Think of the -n object as a completed target. If the action isn't finished yet or is negated, stick with the partitive!

title: Past Tense (Imperfekti) and Stem Changes
subtitle: Forming the simple past tense across verb types
keyPoint: The Finnish simple past (imperfekti) inserts an -i- between the vocalic stem and personal endings, triggering stem vowel mutations such as a/ä dropping or turning into e/o.

useCases.label: Narrative Sequence
useCases.example: Kävelin kotiin ja tein heti ruokaa.

mistakes.note: Check consonant gradation: in 1st person 'nukkua' has a weak stem 'nuku-', yielding 'nukuin'.
Two-syllable stems ending in -a with a first syllable 'o' drop the 'a' before 'i': osta- + i -> osti.
The negative past uses the auxiliary verb (en, et, ei...) + the -nut/-nyt participle, not the imperfekti form.

quiz.question: Yesterday we worked all day (tehdä -> teke-).
quiz.explanation: The past tense of tehdä for 'me' is 'teimme' (stem teke- drops the -e- before past marker -i-).

quiz.question: Where did you (singular) go? (mennä -> mene-)
quiz.explanation: The 2nd person singular past tense marker is -i- + -t, yielding 'menit'.

quiz.question: He gave me the keys (antaa -> anta-).
quiz.explanation: In 2-syllable stems where the first syllable contains 'a', the stem vowel 'a' turns into 'o' before 'i': antoi.

quiz.question: They did not sleep well last night.
quiz.explanation: Negative past with plural 'he' requires 'eivät' followed by the plural past participle 'nukkuneet'.

tip: In the negative past, remember you never use the -i- past form! Instead, use 'en/et/ei...' plus the -nut/-nyt participle.

title: Verb Rections (Rektio)
subtitle: Governing correct case endings on dependent nouns
keyPoint: Finnish verbs require their dependent nouns or objects to appear in specific cases (rections), which must be memorized alongside each verb.

mistakes.note: The verb 'pitää' (to like) requires the elative case (-sta/-stä), not an accusative object.
'Tutustua' (to get to know) requires its target to be in the illative case (mihin/keneen).
'Auttaa' (to help) always demands its object to be in the partitive case.

quiz.question: I like Finnish food. (suomalainen ruoka)
quiz.explanation: 'Pitää' governs the elative case (-sta/-stä): 'suomalaisesta ruoasta'.

quiz.question: She fell in love with Pekka. (rakastua)
quiz.explanation: 'Rakastua' (to fall in love) takes the illative case (mihin/keneen): 'Pekkaan'.

quiz.question: Could you help us? (auttaa + me)
quiz.explanation: 'Auttaa' demands the partitive case: 'meitä'.

quiz.question: We are getting to know our new neighbours. (tutustua + uudet naapurit)
quiz.explanation: 'Tutustua' requires the illative plural: 'uusiin naapureihin'.

tip: Whenever you write down a new Finnish verb, always note down its question word (e.g. 'pitää + mistä?') right beside it.

title: Necessive Clauses ('Täytyy', 'Pitää')
subtitle: Expressing obligation with genitive subjects and fixed verbs
keyPoint: In necessive clauses expressing 'must' or 'have to', the person who must act is in the genitive case (-n), and the modal verb (täytyy, pitää) is fixed in the 3rd person singular.

useCases.label: No Obligation (Negative)
useCases.example: Sinun ei tarvitse maksaa tästä mitään.

useCases.label: Strong Compulsion
useCases.example: Meidän on pakko lähteä heti asemalle.

mistakes.note: The agent in a necessive construction must be in the genitive case ('minun'), never nominative ('minä').
The modal verb 'täytyy' is strictly impersonal and stays 3rd person singular, even with plural agents.
A total object inside a necessive clause takes the nominative-accusative shape, not the genitive -n.

quiz.question: You (singular) must do this task.
quiz.explanation: The subject is genitive ('Sinun'), the verb is fixed ('täytyy'), and total singular objects take the nominative form ('tämä tehtävä') in necessive clauses.

quiz.question: We have to leave now.
quiz.explanation: 'Meidän' is the genitive plural of 'me', followed by the fixed 3rd person singular verb 'pitää'.

quiz.question: You do not need to hurry. (ei tarvitse)
quiz.explanation: In negative necessity clauses, the subject remains genitive ('Sinun') and the negative form is 'ei tarvitse'.

quiz.question: The children must go to bed.
quiz.explanation: The noun 'lapset' must take the genitive plural form 'lasten', paired with the invariant singular 'täytyy'.

tip: Remember the double anomaly: the subject gets a genitive -n, while the total object loses its genitive -n!

title: Passive Voice in the Present Tense
subtitle: Impersonal actions and everyday spoken 'we'
keyPoint: The Finnish present passive omits the specific agent and is universally used in spoken Finnish to replace the first-person plural 'me' form.

cells: one eats / let's eat, one goes
one meets / let's meet, one needs

examples.en: Kaupassa myydään tuoretta leipää joka aamu.

mistakes.note: While 'me menemme' is grammatically correct in formal Finnish, standard colloquial Finnish almost exclusively uses the passive 'me mennään'.
The object of an ongoing impersonal passive action takes the partitive case (suomea), not the nominative.
In the negative present passive, drop the final '-an/-än' ending after the negative auxiliary 'ei'.

quiz.question: How do you say 'We are drinking coffee' in standard spoken Finnish? 'Me ___ kahvia.'
quiz.explanation: 'Me juodaan' uses the passive present form, which functions as colloquial 'we'.

quiz.question: What is the passive present form of 'tehdä' (to do/make)? 'Täällä ___ työtä.'
quiz.explanation: Verb type 2 forms its passive directly from the infinitive stem: teh- + -dään = tehdään.

quiz.question: Which form completes the negative passive: 'Siellä ei ___ englantia.'
quiz.explanation: Negative passive present drops the final vowel length and 'n': 'ei puhuta'.

quiz.question: Convert the suggestion to Finnish: 'Shall we go to sauna?' '___ saunaan?'
quiz.explanation: Adding the question clitic -ko/-kö to the passive form 'mennään' creates a suggestion: 'Mennäänkö?'

tip: Whenever you speak Finnish informally, replace the standard 'me + -mme' ending with 'me + passive'—it instantly makes your speech sound natural!

title: Possessive Suffixes (Omistusliitteet)
subtitle: Marking ownership on nouns and case endings
keyPoint: Possessive suffixes attach to the very end of noun stems and case markers, causing final genitive 'n' or plural 't' consonants to disappear.

mistakes.note: In standard written Finnish, when you use the possessive pronoun 'minun', the noun must take the possessive suffix '-ni'.
When the subject owns the object, the third-person suffix '-nsa/-nsä' must be used on the noun, and the pronoun 'hänen' is omitted.
Case suffixes always precede possessive suffixes: stem + case + possessive suffix (auto + -ssa + -ni).

quiz.question: Select the correct standard form for 'my apartment': 'Tämä on minun ___.'
quiz.explanation: The first-person singular possessive suffix is '-ni', attaching to the vowel stem 'asunto-'.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly places the suffix on 'in your car'?
quiz.explanation: The inessive case '-ssa' comes first, followed by the second-person singular suffix '-si': 'autossasi'.

quiz.question: How do you say 'Anna meets her (own) friend'? 'Anna tapaa ___.'
quiz.explanation: Reflexive third-person possession requires '-nsa/-nsä' on the object noun, without needing 'hänen'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct form for 'our summer cottage': 'Tämä on meidän ___.'
quiz.explanation: The first-person plural possessive suffix corresponding to 'meidän' is '-mme'.

tip: Remember the order of suffixes with the formula: STEM + PLURAL (i) + CASE + POSSESSIVE. The possessive suffix is always the final caboose on the train!

title: The Third Infinitive (MA-Infinitive)
subtitle: Navigating actions with -maan, -massa, and -masta
keyPoint: The MA-infinitive uses internal local case endings to describe moving toward an action (-maan), being engaged in it (-massa), or returning from it (-masta).

examples.en: En voi lähteä töistä syömättä lounasta.

mistakes.note: Movement verbs like 'mennä' require the 3rd infinitive illative (-maan), never the 1st infinitive (basic form).
Do not confuse the state of doing (-massa) with direction; use -massa specifically with static verbs like 'olla'.
The verb 'lakata' (to cease/stop) takes the elative MA-infinitive (-masta), meaning literally 'stopping from doing'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct form for 'We are going to sleep': 'Me menemme ___.'
quiz.explanation: The movement verb 'mennä' governs the illative 3rd infinitive '-maan'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Pekka is currently in the library reading': 'Pekka on kirjastossa ___.'
quiz.explanation: The static auxiliary 'olla' combined with current activity takes inessive '-massa'.

quiz.question: Which verb form completes: 'They just returned from swimming': 'He palasivat juuri ___.'
quiz.explanation: Movement out of or returning from an activity requires the elative '-masta'.

quiz.question: Complete the phrase 'without speaking': 'Hän istui koko illan ___ mitään.'
quiz.explanation: The abessive form '-matta/-mättä' means 'without doing [action]'.

tip: Think of the internal cases: -maan = INTO the action, -massa = INSIDE the action, and -masta = OUT OF the action!

title: VA- and NUT-Participles as Adjectives
subtitle: Compressing relative clauses into pre-nominal attributes
keyPoint: Present (-va/-vä) and past (-nut/-nyt) active participles convert verbs into descriptive adjectives that precede nouns and decline in agreement with them.

mistakes.note: Participles function as pre-nominal modifiers. They go directly before the noun, not after relative pronouns.
The past participle '-nut' changes its stem to '-nee-' before adding case endings: kadonnut -> kadonneen.

mistakes.wrong: laulavat linnut laulavassa metsässä -> laulava linnut
mistakes.note: Like all Finnish adjectives, participial attributes must agree in case and number with the head noun.

quiz.question: How do you express 'a barking dog' as a pre-nominal modifier? 'Pihalla seisoo ___ koira.'
quiz.explanation: The present active participle of 'haukkua' is 'haukkuva', agreeing in nominative singular with 'koira'.

quiz.question: Select the correct form for 'the departed train' (past active nominative): 'Asemalta lähti jo ___ juna.'
quiz.explanation: For an action that has already completed, use the past active participle '-nut/-nyt': 'lähtenyt'.

quiz.question: Transform into the genitive: 'of the crying child' -> '___ lapsen'.
quiz.explanation: The participle agrees in case: 'itkevä' becomes 'itkevän' in the genitive case before 'lapsen'.

quiz.question: What is the stem change of 'väsynyt' (tired) when adding the inessive ending '-ssä'?
quiz.explanation: The suffix '-nut/-nyt' changes to the stem '-nee-' before case endings, yielding 'väsyneessä'.

tip: Using participial attributes instead of 'joka' (who/which) relative clauses is the hallmark of natural B1/B2 level written and formal Finnish!

title: Plural Case Stems (Monikon I-Vartalo)
subtitle: Forming oblique plural cases with the -i- marker
keyPoint: While the nominative plural uses '-t', all other plural cases use the plural marker '-i-' inserted between the vowel stem and the case suffix, triggering specific vowel changes.

mistakes.note: The '-t' plural marker is strictly restricted to the nominative and accusative. All case-bearing plurals use '-i-'.
A single short '-ä' or '-e' drops completely when combined with the plural '-i-'.
Long vowels shorten by losing their first component before the plural '-i-': maa + i + ssa -> maissa.

quiz.question: What is the inessive plural ('in the schools') of 'koulu'?
quiz.explanation: The vowel '-u' remains unchanged before '-i-', resulting in 'koulu-' + '-i-' + '-ssa' = 'kouluissa'.

quiz.question: Form the plural elative ('from the trees') of 'puu':
quiz.explanation: The double vowel 'uu' shortens to single 'u' before the plural '-i-': 'puista'.

quiz.question: What happens to the short '-e' of 'kirje' in the plural adessive ('with letters')?
quiz.explanation: The final short '-e' of the stem drops entirely before '-i-': kirje -> kirj- + -i- + -llä = 'kirjillä'.

quiz.question: Identify the correct plural form of 'vanha katu' in the inessive case ('in old streets'):
quiz.explanation: In 2-syllable stems with 'a' where the first syllable has 'a', the final '-a' shifts to '-o-': vanhoissa; katu has gradation t -> d: kaduissa.

tip: Whenever you spot an '-i-' squeezed right in front of a case ending like '-ssa', '-lla', or '-sta', you are looking at a plural oblique case!

title: The Conditional Mood (Konditionaali)
subtitle: Forming hypothetical sentences and polite requests using -isi-
keyPoint: The conditional mood is formed by inserting the infix -isi- between the strong vowel stem and the personal ending.

useCases.label: Hypothetical Condition
useCases.example: Jos minulla olisi rahaa, matkustaisin Lappiin.

examples.en: Voisitko auttaa minua tämän tehtävän kanssa?
Hän ostaisi uuden auton, jos hänellä olisi varaa.
Me emme tekisi sitä ilman sinua.
Olisin tullut eilen, jos olisin tiennyt juhlista.

mistakes.wrong: Jos minä tietäisin, minä sanon sinulle.
mistakes.right: Jos minä tietäisin, minä sanoisin sinulle.
mistakes.note: Both clauses in a conditional sentence typically require the conditional mood in Finnish, unlike in English where the 'then' clause uses 'would'.
Polite requests use the question clitic -ko/-kö directly attached to the conditional verb instead of relying solely on intonation or word order.
Do not switch back to the present indicative in the consequence clause of an unreal hypothetical situation.

quiz.question: Jos minulla ___ aikaa, lukisin enemmän kirjoja.
quiz.explanation: The condition clause takes the conditional form 'olisi' with the third-person singular in possessive constructions.

quiz.question: ___ sinä sulkea ikkunan, kiitos?
quiz.explanation: For a polite request, use the conditional form with the question suffix: 'Voisitko' (Could you).

quiz.question: Me ___ mielellämme mukaan konserttiin.
quiz.explanation: First-person plural conditional takes the marker -isi- plus the ending -mme: 'tulisimme' (we would come).

quiz.question: Jos he tietäisivät osoitteen, he ___ meille kirjeen.
quiz.explanation: Third-person plural conditional adds -isi- followed by -vat: 'kirjoittaisivat' (they would write).

tip: Long vowels shorten before the infix: aa/ää drops the first vowel (ottaa -> ott- + isi -> ottaisi), while diphthongs ending in -i lose the first element (voida -> vo- + isi -> voisi).

title: Clause Equivalents (Lauseenvastikkeet)
subtitle: Compress 'että' and 'kun' clauses into elegant participial phrases
keyPoint: Finnish shortens subordinate clauses by replacing 'että' with the participle genitive and 'kun' with the second infinitive in the inessive case.

useCases.label: Simultaneous Actions (Kun)
useCases.example: Kotiin tullessani huomasin ikkunan olevan auki.

useCases.label: Past State Perception (Että + past)
useCases.example: He luulivat meidän jo lähteneen kotiin.

mistakes.note: Never keep the conjunction 'kun' or 'että' when converting to a participle clause equivalent.
Drop 'että' and put the agent in the genitive case ('hänen') before the participle.
Do not add a genitive pronoun like 'minun' before the verb if the subject is the same; use only the possessive suffix '-ni'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct equivalent for: 'Kun tulin kotiin, söin heti.'
quiz.explanation: With the same subject (I), use the inessive of the 2nd infinitive ('tullessa') plus the 1st person possessive suffix '-ni'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct equivalent for: 'Luulin, että sinä tiesit vastauksen.'
quiz.explanation: Because the subordinate clause verb was in the past tense ('tiesit'), use the past active participle in genitive: 'sinun tietäneen'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence to mean 'When the sun rose...': 'Auringon ___ heräsimme retkellä.'
quiz.explanation: 'Auringon noustessa' is the temporal clause equivalent for intransitive 'aurinko nousee' (2nd infinitive inessive: nousta -> nouste- -> noustessa).

quiz.question: Choose the correct equivalent for: 'Hän sanoi, että hän lähtee huomenna.' (same person)
quiz.explanation: When the reporting subject and the actor are the same person, use the reflexive possessive suffix '-nsä' instead of a separate genitive pronoun.

tip: Remember the agent rule: if the agent in the shortcut clause is different from the main clause subject, put that agent in the genitive case (e.g., 'äidin tullessa', 'hänen tietävän').

title: Marginal Cases: Abessive, Comitative, and Instructive
subtitle: Expressing lack, accompaniment, and manner with specialized case endings
keyPoint: The abessive (-tta/-ttä) indicates absence, the comitative (-ineen) marks accompaniment and always requires a possessive suffix, while the instructive (-n) conveys manner or means and almost always appears in the plural.

useCases.label: Abessive: Without something
useCases.example: Hän jäi sanattomaksi ja lähti kotiin luvatta.

mistakes.note: The comitative ending -ine- must always be followed by a possessive suffix, usually -en (3rd person) or matching the subject.
Idiomatic instructive expressions describing body parts or sensory means are typically formed in the plural with -n.
Do not double up the preposition 'ilman' with the abessive suffix '-tta'; use either 'ilman rahaa' (with partitive) or 'rahatta' alone.

quiz.question: Choose the correct comitative form: 'Presidentti saapui juhlaan ___.' (with his wife)
quiz.explanation: The comitative case uses the plural marker -i-, suffix -ne-, and a possessive suffix: rouva -> rouvineen.

quiz.question: Complete the instructive idiom: 'Hän puolusti kantaansa kynsin ja ___.' (with teeth)
quiz.explanation: The set instructive expression 'kynsin ja hampain' (tooth and nail) requires the instructive plural 'hampain'.

quiz.question: Which abessive form means 'without permission'?
quiz.explanation: The singular abessive of 'lupa' uses the weak stem 'luva-' plus the suffix '-tta', yielding 'luvatta'.

quiz.question: Select the correct sentence expressing 'We walked barefoot':
quiz.explanation: The plural instructive case ending '-n' modifies both the adjective and noun: 'paljain jaloin'.

tip: In modern spoken Finnish, people prefer 'ilman + partitive' over the abessive and 'kanssa + genitive' over the comitative; save these marginal cases for formal writing, literature, and fixed idioms.

title: The Agent Participle (Agenttipartisiippi)
subtitle: Forming relative-like modifiers with '-ma/-mä' and a genitive agent
keyPoint: The agent participle suffix '-ma/-mä' combines with an agent in the genitive case or a possessive suffix to replace a relative clause meaning 'done by someone'.

cells: Noun agent in genitive + -ma/-mä + head noun
the book (that was) bought by me
the decision not made by the government
Inflected head noun (participle agrees in case)
in the car repaired by father

examples.en: Luin eilen sinun suosittelemasi kirjan loppuun.

mistakes.note: The agent must always be in the genitive case (äidin), not the nominative (äiti).
When the agent is a personal pronoun, the participle must take the corresponding possessive suffix (-ni for 'my').
The participle functions as an adjective and must agree in case and number with the head noun (kirjan -> kirjoittaman).

quiz.question: Choose the correct phrase: 'the coffee made by Maija'
quiz.explanation: The agent takes the genitive form ('Maijan') followed by the -mA participle ('keittämä') and the modified noun.

quiz.question: Choose the correct translation: 'the car (that was) repaired by me'
quiz.explanation: With a 1st person agent, use the possessive suffix '-ni' on the participle ('korjaamani'). The pronoun 'minun' is optional.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Asumme Alvar Aallon ___ talossa.' (We live in a house designed by Alvar Aalto.)
quiz.explanation: The head noun 'talossa' is in the inessive case (-ssa), so the agent participle must agree with it: 'suunnittelemassa'.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly means 'the homework not done by the student'?
quiz.explanation: The negative form of the agent participle uses the caritive suffix '-maton/-mätön' with the genitive agent ('oppilaan tekemätön läksy').

tip: Think of the agent participle as a compact alternative to a relative clause: instead of 'ruoka, jonka äiti teki', say 'äidin tekemä ruoka' to sound much more natural and fluent in formal or written Finnish.

title: The Potential Mood (Potentiaali)
subtitle: Expressing probability, doubt, and formal speculation using -ne-
keyPoint: The potential mood expresses probability or speculation using the marker -ne- (which assimilates to -le-, -re-, or -se- depending on the verb stem) in formal or literary Finnish.

useCases.label: Formal or journalistic speculation
useCases.example: Hallitus tehnee päätöksen asiasta ensi viikolla.

examples.en: Hän tietänee vastauksen paremmin kuin me.
Emme liene valmiita näin suureen muutokseen.

mistakes.note: When the consonant stem ends in 'l', 'r', or 's', the marker '-ne-' assimilates to '-le-', '-re-', or '-se-'. Never keep '-ne-' after these consonants.
The verb 'olla' has an irregular suppletive potential stem based on 'liene-', never 'ollene-'.
In negative forms, the auxiliary 'ei' takes the personal ending, while the main verb drops personal suffixes and keeps only the potential stem (tienne).

quiz.question: The train will probably arrive late today: 'Juna ___ tänään myöhässä.'
quiz.explanation: Type 1 verb 'saapua' takes the vowel stem 'saapu-' + potential marker '-ne-' + 3rd person singular ending '-e', forming 'saapunee'.

quiz.question: Which form correctly replaces 'varmaan on' in formal register? 'Hän ___ oikeassa.'
quiz.explanation: 'Olla' forms its potential mood irregularly using the stem 'liene-'. The 3rd person singular is 'lienee'.

quiz.question: Complete with the potential form of 'tulla' (she will probably come): 'Hän ___ huomenna.'
quiz.explanation: In Type 2 verbs with an 'l' stem like 'tulla' (stem 'tul-'), the suffix '-ne-' assimilates completely to '-le-', yielding 'tullee'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct negative potential form: 'Me emme ___ tätä ongelmaa vielä.'
quiz.explanation: In negative potential sentences with a plural subject, the main verb appears in the bare potential stem 'ratkaissee' without personal suffix attached.

tip: In everyday spoken Finnish, people almost always use adverbs like 'varmaan' or 'ehkä' instead of the potential mood, but mastering '-ne-' is essential for reading news, academic articles, and literature.
